claim: Evidence that fits every hypothesis equally has no discriminating value; the useful quantity is how much more likely the item is under one hypothesis than under its rival (a likelihood ratio). Heuer states this in words and a matrix; Good and Fischhoff-Beyth-Marom give the formal version (those two not opened).
agent_test: At equal tokens, compare (i) plain pick-the-best-hypothesis with (ii) a step that has the model rate each evidence item under each hypothesis, then code drops items with equal ratings across hypotheses before choosing. Score on cases where one item is the decider.

claim: People ask for more data about the hypothesis they already hold instead of the matching data under the rival (pseudodiagnosticity). Replications give only 30-31% correct choice in one family, and 43% in another; the size depends on task features (rarity, perceived informativeness), and a formal reanalysis says part of the 'error' is a misapplied norm. Gap search: Kern and Doherty (1982, abstract only) found 83% of 65 senior medical students chose non-required same-hypothesis information; Anderson and Doherty (2024, abstract only) found the bias persists when no percentages are shown, so it is a search habit and not only a misreading of numbers. The Doherty 1979 percentages are still unobtained.
agent_test: Build 2x2 likelihood-request items (Doherty style, equal ratio, rare/common feature). Measure whether the agent requests the rival cell. Compare plain, and a scaffold line that forces 'name the rival likelihood for this same datum'.

claim: In rule discovery, people mostly test cases their hypothesis predicts; only 6 of 29 (Wason) and 0 of 51 (replication) named the right rule on first announcement. LLMs show the same: instruction-tuned models use 66-82% positive tests, reasoning models 24-39%, and success tracks fewer positive tests (rho = -0.779).
agent_test: Run Wason 2-4-6 style and FalsifyBench-style games at fixed token budget: plain vs scaffold that requires one test chosen to be false if the hypothesis is true. Report positive-test share and success.
audit_note: Minor: the human figures are Heuer's secondary report of Wason and a repeat, and the 24-39% range spans the reasoning models listed (e.g. GPT-OSS-20B 24.2%, GPT-5-Mini 39.0%).

claim: The ACH matrix as a whole has not been shown to improve accuracy or coherence. Randomised tests: 50 UK analysts (MAE 0.26 ACH vs 0.21 control, p=.14), 227 panelists (no coherence gain, less reliable across isomorphic cases), 159 psychology students (no effect on credibility ratings), 39 mixed (no reduction of serial-position or confirmation bias). A critical review of 7 articles/6 experiments concludes little to no benefit and possible harm.
agent_test: Treat the full matrix as unproven under G7. Test at equal tokens: matrix scaffold vs plain vs 'list all cues and rate usefulness only' on a probabilistic multi-cue task (tribes task) and on analyst-style items.
audit_note: Minor: Karvetski and Mandel is listed twice (one study), Mandel's group authored the 2018 and 2020 studies and the review, and the 'less reliable' result is p=.051 (MAD .22 vs .18).

claim: Parts of ACH may help: ACH analysts rated how useful each cue was far better (mean within-person r = .68 vs .17), and listed all cues more often. But the better ratings did not carry to final accuracy (r = -.10 in ACH, -.42 in control).
agent_test: Add a 'rate each cue usefulness' step and test whether code that uses those ratings (not the model) to weight cues beats the model combining them itself.

claim: When ACH users scored uncertain evidence, evidence rated non-diagnostic still moved the score, with about 30-32% of the impact of fully diagnostic evidence (intercept .233, slope .502, R2 = .055). Measured in the ACH arm only, on the matrix consistency score, not on the final probability.
agent_test: Check whether the agent matrix ratings leak weight from equal-rated items: regress its final pick on differential rating; drop equal-rated items in code and see if accuracy changes.

claim: ACH users double-count a cue that is perfectly correlated with an earlier one (25% low salience, 57% high salience, N=147); a factorised-Bayes method also failed on correlated evidence.
agent_test: Feed the agent cases with duplicated or derived cues; measure double counting; test a code step that clusters cues by shared source before weighing.

claim: Layout of evidence changes strategy: hypotheses in rows led to fewer choices of the consistency-favoured hypothesis (39.2%) than ACH-style columns (61.8%) or text (67.3%), N=161. Among 62 Dutch military analysts, 66.1% balanced, 19.4% leaned on consistency, 14.5% on inconsistency.
agent_test: Present the same evidence to the agent in three layouts (per-hypothesis rows, per-evidence rows, prose) and check whether choice changes; if so fix the layout in code.

claim: Probability judgments on a set of exclusive hypotheses are incoherent: analysts four probabilities summed to 1.54 (control) and 1.77 (ACH); panelists were subadditive on two hypotheses; 91.9% of Dutch analysts were nonadditive.
agent_test: Ask the agent for raw probabilities over exclusive hypotheses, measure the sum, then compare raw vs code-normalised answers on the same items.
audit_note: Minor: the 91.9% is for the Dutch military analysts/cadets sample (N=62) and sums over 1 are called subadditive in these papers.

claim: Forcing coherence in code (normalise to sum 1) and averaging independent judgments cuts error a lot (raw MAE .23 to .15 after coherentising; .09 after also averaging 50 analysts), but most of the aggregation gain is variance reduction, because random responses gained about as much.
agent_test: Replicate on the agent: raw vs coherentised vs coherentised-and-averaged over N fresh samples, at equal tokens; include a random-response baseline so variance reduction is not mistaken for skill.
audit_note: Minor: .23 to .15 is the paper's own coherentization (plain normalisation to sum 1 would have given about .13), and both sources are from the same group (Mandel, Karvetski); random-response comparison (aggregation gain comparable to random data) is confirmed.

claim: Prompted LLMs pick weak next queries: Prompt-Only 20 Questions success 8-45% (Animals) and 10-34% (Things); 14.6-18.5% of Battleship questions had zero information gain; the best model solved 28% of WILT rules; 40-50% on QuestBench logic/planning; and Ling clinical models fell from 73.5% to 33.1% when they had to request the evidence.
agent_test: Build a query-selection probe (hidden-hypothesis game with a known hypothesis set) and measure prompt-only success at fixed turns as the base number for any scaffold element.
audit_note: Minor: 14.6-18.5% zero-information-gain questions are the two example models named in the Battleship paper (GPT-4o, Llama-4-Scout), not a range across all models; the Ling 73.5 to 33.1 is one cohort at k=3 requests.

claim: Choosing the next query by expected information gain, with the LLM supplying likelihoods or candidate answers and code doing the arithmetic, beats letting the LLM pick: BED-LLM +37.4 points mean (Things GPT-4o 34 to 64), UoT +38.1% mean, Battleship small models beat humans, and code-task disambiguation improves. Gains shrink for stronger models and non-game tasks. Gap search: Prompts to Posteriors (2026) re-ran BED-LLM against a one-prompt in-context EIG recipe on three current open reasoning models and found the naive recipe matched it, so the code-side advantage shown on 2024 models may not hold for reasoning modes.
agent_test: At equal tokens, implement a code-side EIG pick over a model-listed candidate set with model-supplied yes/no likelihoods; compare to prompt-only and to the Split baseline on the same probe. Count all sampling calls in the budget.

claim: A crude balanced-split rule already gets much of the gain (Animals GPT-4o-mini: Prompt-Only 44, Split 78, BED-LLM 88; Llama-3.1-8B 8, 49, 63). Full EIG with a noisy likelihood adds a further 10-14 points over Split here; free CoT adds 2-17 over Prompt-Only on Animals (Mistral-Large 33 to 35, GPT-4o 45 to 62). Gap search: no equal-token test on non-guessing tasks was found; Wild Guesses (2026) shows EIG on model-written programs loses to a positive-test rule on simple concepts.
agent_test: Test Split alone first (cheapest). Keep full EIG only if it beats Split at equal tokens on our probe.

claim: Free-text structure alone gives small or mixed gains: CoT lifted 20 Questions unevenly (GPT-4o-mini 44 to 55, Mistral-Large 33 to 35), CoT did not fix belief updating, yet a required ranked hypothesis table raised root-cause top-1 from 83.2 to 87.6 and counterfactual critique plus structured investigation were the largest ablation costs (about 5 to 6 points).
agent_test: Compare at equal tokens: free CoT vs required hypothesis table vs table plus 'what single finding would reject the leader' on a diagnosis-style item set.

claim: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly from sequential evidence: flight-preference accuracy plateaus near 36-58% against 81% for an exact Bayesian assistant; separate-conversation probabilities violated Dutch-book tests in over 50% of scenarios; small models under-update and large ones over-update; the elicitation protocol changes the answer.
agent_test: Do not let the model do the posterior arithmetic; measure its raw updates on bookbag-style items to size the gap.
audit_note: Minor: the 36-58% vs 81% flight figures are not stated in the Qiu text I could read (plateau after round 1 is), and the small-under/large-over update pattern is specific to BayesBench's coin task; Dutch-book over 50% across separate conversations is confirmed.

claim: The gap in belief updating can be closed without training by moving the posterior into code or a tool: Python tool and reasoning mode brought KL near 0 on toy worlds, and AdaptFuse (symbolic posterior, frozen LLM) reached 76.2% vs 73.4% Bayesian-teaching fine-tuning and 44.7% self-consistency. It needs a hand-specified likelihood and hypothesis set.
agent_test: Give the agent a code posterior over the hypothesis list it generates (model supplies likelihood estimates as numbers, code multiplies). Compare final pick to model-only reasoning at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: 76.2/73.4/44.7 are Gemma figures (AdaptFuse is labelled the legacy EMA configuration; the no-EMA ablation gives 74.0), and the Python tool result is Gemini-2.5-Pro on ProteinWorld-hard.

claim: Probabilities read from token logits or verbalised confidence were near chance as diagnostic estimates (AUROC about 50 for two open models, medical tabular tasks).
agent_test: Check verbalised and logit confidence against hit rates on our items before any stop rule uses them.

claim: Reasoning models test more outside their hypothesis and succeed more (GPT-5.2-Chat 75% vs best instruction-tuned 41%; thinking modes gained more from debiasing prompts), but 2024 reasoning models did not dominate WILT (o1-preview 12/50 vs Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14/50), and bias alone is not enough: conclusive falsification rate correlates -0.937 with bias. Gap search: in Jhaveri et al. thinking mode raised success but did not consistently raise the share of tests outside the current guess, so the thinking gain is not only less confirmation.
agent_test: Run the same falsification probe in direct, short-reason and long-reason modes, to see where extra thinking buys negative tests.

claim: A prompt that tells the model to test the opposite of its last test (Think-in-Opposites) raised rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average across 11 LLMs, and helped every model-mode pair; Dual-Goal helped thinking models (8 of 11 cells) but cut success for several non-thinking ones (Qwen3-14B 23% to 13%, Qwen3-32B 33% to 10%). In a second task (Blicket) TiO helped thinking models (Qwen3-32B 57% to 86%) but not all non-thinking ones (Qwen3-32B 64% to 56%). No equal-token control: thinking-mode tokens per turn rose 20-100%.
agent_test: Add one TiO line to S7 and compare at equal tokens on thinking and non-thinking modes, on both number-rule items and a non-numeric item set; do not use the Dual-Goal wording on non-thinking modes.

claim: When the evidence supplied to a person is sampled to fit their stated hypothesis, they grow more confident without getting closer to the truth. With 557 people, discovery fell from 29.5% (random feedback) to 5.9% with a default GPT chatbot; default GPT was statistically equivalent to explicit rule-confirming feedback. In a clue-selection pilot, models picked suspicion-leaning sentences 25 times and exoneration-leaning 0 times.
agent_test: Input hygiene: strip the user preferred hypothesis from the evidence-gathering prompt; compare queries chosen with and without the stated hypothesis in context.

claim: Failure to use negated or absent findings is where LLM diagnosis audits show shortcut-like errors, although most evidence interactions are faithful support or conflict (86.6-89.6% of interaction strength).
agent_test: Add probes where the decisive finding is an absence; check whether the agent counts absence as evidence.

claim: The gap between having evidence and asking for it is not explained by the amount of evidence: count-matched hindsight reaches 63.0% vs Foresight 33.1% at k=3 (gap 29.8 points, CI 22.1-37.6; 28.7 at k=6). Within the same cases, swapping the foresight fact set for the hindsight-selected set adds 26.7 points and reordering the same foresight set adds 9.3, while reversing the hindsight order costs 26.0, so it is mostly WHICH facts, with order second. Only 16.0% of the retrospectively top-ranked facts are recovered at k=3. Adding one top-ranked fact to a wrong foresight state rescued +38.8 points over a control fact. Caveat: the reference facts are chosen by an LLM selector with hindsight; one preprint under review.
agent_test: On a case set with one planted decisive item among N, compare plain choice with a code-ranked request list scored by separation across hypotheses; count how often the decisive item is requested by k=3 and compare with the 16.0% recall seen here.

claim: Models keep a longer candidate pool than they use: in an investigation agent the best pool scored 89.2 but the selected answer 79.2, so selection, not generation, was the bottleneck.
agent_test: Measure oracle-in-pool vs selected accuracy for our agent; if the gap is large, put the effort into the discriminating test, not more generation.

claim: Language models show human-like content effects on the Wason selection task: better on realistic than abstract rules (z > 2.2 for Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 and humans).
agent_test: Reword abstract discrimination tasks into concrete forms and see if the agent test choice improves.

claim: An ACH-inspired matrix prompt added only about +2.3 points on multiple-choice answer aggregation without training; the larger gain (+7 to +7.8) came from training. No test of the matrix alone as a scaffold on evidence-weighing tasks was found.
agent_test: This is the missing direct test: ACH matrix vs plain at equal tokens on analyst-style multi-cue items.

claim: Code-side expected information gain over a model-generated hypothesis pool is not a free win. In an LLM-proposed program space it beat random and a positive-test rule only on compound rules (multiples of 3 or 7: 8 queries vs DNF vs 13; odd multiples of 3: 14 vs 35 vs 21) and was worse on simple rules (multiples of 4: 7 vs 4 vs 2), because highly diagnostic queries moved the posterior outside the support where the model proposes valid programs. Hard rules mostly failed for all methods. One workshop paper, apparently one run per cell.
agent_test: On self-generated hypothesis lists, compare plain choice, a balanced-split rule, and EIG, at equal calls and tokens; track how often the model rejects or cannot score the hypotheses after a decisive test. Try a switch: cheap tests first, EIG when no progress for two rounds.

claim: A large share of evidence requests add nothing: 25.3% repeat an observed fact and 16.0% match nothing, so only 58.7% of request slots give a new unique fact (three requests give 2.09 facts). Recovery is partial (42.8% after a duplicate, 34.2% after a no-match) and depends on type: after a duplicate, switching category recovers 49.7% vs 17.1% for staying; after a no-match, staying recovers 65.4% vs 27.6%. A fixed menu of targets did not beat free-form (31.7% both at k=3). No test of a hard code block on repeats exists.
agent_test: Add a code-side request ledger that rejects exact repeats and, after a repeat, forces a different evidence category; measure unique-fact rate and final accuracy at equal request budget.

claim: Models are directionally right but weak at turning evidence into numbers. Base models' updates correlate with the shift implied by their own likelihoods (BCC 0.48-0.74) but with slopes of only 0.30-0.48 (under-update), and direction agreement is 64-76%. Elicited probabilities are incoherent across separate chats (above 50% Dutch-book violation rate) and about 10% or less within one dialogue. Without reasoning, posteriors drift from the oracle within a few pieces of evidence; with reasoning they match closed-form posteriors, and with code they match hard ones. These tests supply the likelihoods; they do not test whether the model can supply sound P(E|H) for real analytic evidence.
agent_test: Collect model-rated likelihood ratios for items with known answers, compare them with the model's direct posterior and with a code pooled posterior, in one dialogue and in a reasoning mode, and report accuracy and Brier score.
audit_note: BCC 0.477-0.743, gradients 0.295-0.482, direction agreement 63.7-75.8% (Imran et al. Table 1); Filbry et al. cross-chat Dutch-book violations above 50% of 30 scenarios, within-dialogue 10% (Gemini) or 1 of 30 (Gemma), reasoning and code results match; Wu 2026 not needed; the abstract page alone did not show these numbers, full text did.

claim: Across forecasting, value-laden and paper-review tasks, LLM belief updates were predictable from the model's own prior belief (Martingale scores with chain of thought 0.037 forecasting, 0.086 paper review, 0.103 ChangeMyView), and a score near 0.04 coincided with forecasts worse than chance; prompting to conform to the prior generally raised the score and a critical-thinking prompt lowered it only for some models. Separately, in BayesBench's social-judgment task, actively engaging with a simulated user produced a persistent pro-user bias that passive reading of the same evidence did not. Neither study tested removing the stance at the evidence-search step.
agent_test: Run the evidence-request step twice, once with the user's hypothesis in context and once with a neutral list of all hypotheses; compare the share of requests that only address the stated hypothesis.
audit_note: Martingale scores (0.037, 0.086, 0.103), the ~0.04 worse-than-chance remark and the BayesBench active-vs-passive pro-user bias all check out, but Table 1 of He et al. shows the system-prompt effects are not consistent across models in forecasting (critical-thinking prompt raised the score for GPT-4o and Maverick and lowered it for R1, Flash and Scout; prior-conforming raised it for most but not Gemini Flash), and the Martingale result concerns the model's own prior belief, not a user-stated stance.
claim_before_audit: A stated stance anchors the model. Across forecasting, value-laden and paper-review tasks, belief updates were predictable from the prior (Martingale score 0.037 forecasting, 0.086 paper review, 0.103 ChangeMyView with chain of thought) and a score near 0.04 coincided with forecasts worse than chance; a prior-conforming prompt increased it and a critical-thinking prompt reduced it in forecasting. Separately, active engagement with a stance-holding simulated user produced a persistent pro-user bias that passive reading of the same evidence did not. Neither study tested removing the stance at the evidence-search step.

claim: Decisive items are missed and exculpatory items are skipped. In a mystery-reading pilot, 31 of 37 runs chose the same wrong trio, suspicion-oriented sentences were chosen 25 times and adjacent exoneration-oriented ones 0 times, and clue hits did not predict correct answers (the model with most clue hits named fewest correct people). In clinical vignettes, one added top-ranked fact rescued +38.8 points. The mystery study is a two-story pilot with author-defined clues.
agent_test: Plant one exculpatory item among many; compare plain, per-item scoring against every hypothesis, and per-item scoring with code-side dropping of items with equal scores; report the share of runs that use the exculpatory item.

claim: A short teaching intervention (competing-hypotheses heuristic plus Bayes' theorem) reduced pseudodiagnostic data choices in medical students: intervention n=119 vs control n=89, similar at baseline, better after training at p<.001 (abstract only; effect size unknown; nonequivalent groups). No LLM test of the same instruction exists.
agent_test: Run Doherty-style likelihood-request items with and without a line that says to name the rival hypothesis and its likelihood; compare choice of the rival cell at equal tokens.
